source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: budget-aware evaluation of LLM reasoning strategies
finding: At matched budget, plain chain-of-thought self-consistency beat multi-agent debate and Reflexion on five datasets. ToT was tested only on Game of 24: with GPT-4 it beat the other strategies even when budget was counted; with GPT-3.5 simple self-consistency beat it by a wide margin.
numbers: Budget per question capped at 20 queries or 10k tokens for SC, debate (6 agents x 3 rounds = 18 queries), Reflexion (up to 19 queries). GPT-3.5 used for the 5-dataset runs (GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, HotpotQA, CSQA). ToT Game of 24 numbers are in figures only; the text gives no exact percentages for the ToT-vs-SC gap.
quote: On weaker models than GPT-4, it is still better to use simpler strategies like SC
limits: Search type is ToT with an LLM self-evaluator, not a coded checker. Game of 24 only for ToT. For GPT-3.5 the authors used a modified evaluation prompt that gave much better results than the default. Exact ToT-vs-SC numbers not in text.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 5: the one matched-budget ToT study says search needs a strong model. On the weaker model, spend the budget on sampling. It never used a coded checker, so the gap-1 question is still open.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies - ToT proposer and evaluator ablation (Game of 24, Fig 8)
finding: In ToT, evaluator quality matters, but a cheap evaluator keeps most of the gain. A random evaluator made accuracy fall steeply. Evaluating each thought once instead of three times also dropped accuracy. A weak GPT-3.5 proposer with a GPT-4 evaluator got only 0.38, so the proposer matters as much.
numbers: 100 Game of 24 instances, beam width 5: GPT-4 proposer + GPT-3.5 evaluator $33.53, 72%; GPT-4 proposer + GPT-4 evaluator $159.87, 76%. At b=1 with GPT-4 evaluator: $49.9, 65%. GPT-3.5 proposer + GPT-4 evaluator: 0.38. Prices as of Aug 2023.
quote: Evaluator quality has a non-trivial impact
limits: Single task, 100 items, one run per setting as far as the text shows. Prices are old. No arm replaces the search by resampling with the same evaluator.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: gives a partial split. Evaluator and proposer both carry weight, and the evaluator can be cheap. The clean test (same evaluator, resampling instead of tree) is still missing.

source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang (2025) Inference Scaling Laws: compute-optimal inference for LLM problem-solving (ICLR 2025)
finding: With a reward model, MCTS lost to plain sampling at every compute budget because its rollouts are costly. A reward-balanced tree search (REBASE) beat sampling at lower compute. Sampling with voting saturates at a ceiling set by the model.
numbers: MATH500, weighted voting. Mistral-7B: sampling 8.70e14 FLOPs 42.8% vs REBASE 1.36e14 FLOPs 45.0%. Llemma-7B: sampling 10.0e14 FLOPs 45.5% vs REBASE 1.48e14 FLOPs 46.8%. Llemma-34B: sampling 12.1e14 FLOPs 46.7% vs REBASE 7.08e14 FLOPs 49.2%. Paper says REBASE reaches higher accuracy with about 7x less compute for the 7B model.
quote: MCTS underperforms the sampling-based methods at each compute budget
limits: Needs a trained process reward model, which a prompt-only agent lacks. Math word problems, not planning. Sample counts per table row are garbled in the PDF text (it reads 256 vs 32); trust the FLOPs. Authors say the 7x finding differs from earlier tree-search work that cost more than voting.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: shows the answer depends on the kind of search. Naive MCTS loses to sampling at equal compute. Budget-aware, evaluator-guided expansion can win. Test our search against sampling per FLOP or per dollar, never per accuracy alone.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Inference Scaling Laws - model size and difficulty
finding: A smaller model with a good inference strategy can beat a larger model at the same compute, until the small model saturates. Tree search helps most on hard problems; on easy ones it ties sampling.
numbers: Llemma-7B + REBASE beats Llemma-34B across tested strategies on MATH500 (abstract). Llemma-7B beat 34B until 128 samples were drawn. MATH-easy (levels 1-2): sampling and REBASE comparable. MATH-hard (levels 3-5): REBASE significant advantage (figures only).
quote: performance of sampling and REBASE on easy problems (levels 1-2) is comparable
limits: Fine-tuned Llemma and Mistral-7B, math only. The text gives difficulty effects as figure descriptions, not numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and 6: against the 19% vs 74% GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 ToT result, here the small model gains the most from search. A rule that fits both: small models gain when the evaluator is strong and the task is checkable; they fail when the small model must also propose and judge thoughts.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Search with a process verifier hurts on easy questions and helps on medium ones. On easy questions (levels 1-2) beam search got worse as budget rose, because it over-exploits the verifier. On levels 3-4 beam search consistently beat best-of-N. On level 5 nothing made real progress. Choosing the strategy by predicted difficulty matched best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S* base. Compute-optimal allocation: up to 4x less test-time compute than best-of-N (e.g. 64 vs 256 samples) for revisions and for PRM search. FLOPs-matched against a 14x larger pretrained model: test-time compute preferable on easy and medium questions, pretraining preferable on the hardest. Difficulty bins from the model's own pass rate predicted gains better than the MATH labels.
quote: on the easy questions (levels 1 and 2), the stronger optimizer of the two approaches, beam search, degrades performance
limits: Needs a trained verifier. Difficulty bins used 2-fold cross-validation on the test set. PaLM 2 is not the model we would deploy.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the clearest gating evidence. Gate on a model-specific difficulty estimate from a cheap pass. Do not search on items the cheap pass already gets right, since search can lower accuracy there.

source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi (2024) Thought of Search - what the LLM wrote and how many tries it took
finding: GPT-4 wrote the successor function and goal test as Python. The successor function usually needed more than one try. Mistakes were mostly missing corner cases and shallow vs deep copy bugs, fixed after the exact error was fed back.
numbers: Average LLM interactions until a correct pair: 24 game 1.2 (successor) and 1 (goal); mini crosswords 2.4 and 1.4; BlocksWorld 2.8 and 1; PrOntoQA 1.6 and 1. Five repeats per domain. Every generated pair then solved 100%: 1361 of 1362 24-game cases plus the one unsolvable, 20 of 20 crosswords, 502 BlocksWorld, 4000 PrOntoQA.
limits: A human gave minor help and feedback in the loop. Authors note the model's mistakes repeat across runs. Domains have crisp, short rule texts.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: first-try failure is common for the successor function (average 1.2 to 2.8 tries), rare for the goal test. Plan a test-and-repair loop around generated operators.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search - limits stated in the paper
finding: The crossword run assumed the clue answers were given: each clue had 10 candidate words including the right one. The search was then coded. The paper warns larger BlocksWorld instances would need a heuristic.
numbers: Crossword: 20 games solved by all 5 pairs, 5.5 s to 346 s depending on successor efficiency. ToT on the same set: up to 200 LLM calls per game with a bound of 100 expansions. BlocksWorld sets have only 4 to 5 blocks. Cost estimate $40 IO/CoT, $200 ReAct, $14,000 RAP, $16,000 LATS (500 input and 50 output tokens per call, GPT-4-turbo prices).
limits: The crossword comparison to ToT is not like for like, since candidate generation was given. Cost figures are the authors' estimate, not measured spend.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: code-as-operator solved the search part when the world is formal. It does not show transfer to tasks where the rules are fuzzy; every tested domain has an exact rule text.

source: Cao, Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi (2024/2025) Automating Thought of Search (AutoToS)
finding: Automatic unit-test feedback replaces the human. Calls to the model until soundness and completeness tests pass: the minimum is 2 (one per function), so every average above 2 means the first try failed on some runs.
numbers: Average LLM calls, 5 repeats, cap 10 per function. GPT-4o: 24 Game 3.4, PrOntoQA 2.6, Sokoban 2.2, Crossword 5.8, BlocksWorld 2.0. GPT-4o-mini: 8.8, 4.8, 6.4, 9.6, 10.0. Llama3.1-70b: 7.4, 2.0, 8.2, 6.2, 5.8. Llama3.1-405b: 3.4, 2.0, 2.6, 4.0, 3.2. Accuracy reached 100% on all domains after feedback.
limits: Only five puzzle or planning domains with small unit-test sets (up to 10 instances). Llama3-70b, Mistral 7x8b and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite were tried and dropped as performing poorly. Open models were run via chat interface.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 5: first-try pass rates are modest even for large models, and smaller models need several repairs. Budget 2 to 10 calls for operator code, and keep the checks that gate it.

source: Cao et al. (2025) AutoToS - error types and bloopers
finding: Most code errors were failed successor soundness and completeness tests. Smaller models made more kinds of error. A partial soundness test (for example, at most 5 letters filled per crossword move) caught bugs that unit tests missed.
numbers: The error-count chart is a figure; the text reports that the majority of errors are failed successor soundness and completeness tests. DeepSeek-Coder-V2 rarely raised exceptions or changed the input state.
limits: Domain-specific tests were hand written (3 invented states per test). Count of failures per type not available as text.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the test set for generated operators is the real cost. For messy tasks we would need to write those tests too.

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors (MAKER)
finding: Towers of Hanoi with 20 disks (about 1.05 million moves) was solved with zero errors by splitting the task into single-move calls, passing the current disk state to each call, putting the strategy in the prompt, and voting per step. This shows the earlier collapse is not a hard limit when the step is small and checked.
numbers: gpt-4.1-mini, max 750 output tokens, red-flagging of malformed output, first-to-ahead-by-k voting with k_min=3 (projected cost $3.5K at 95% target; paper). Per-step error rate stable from 10 to 20 disks (mean 0.0045 for gpt-4.1-mini at temperature 0.1, 0.0017 for o3-mini). gpt-4.1-nano mean error 0.3583 (k_min 29, $41.9K). One reported full run.
quote: the per-step error rate is remarkably stable as the number of disks increases
limits: Algorithm is handed to the model, so it tests execution, not insight. Each agent writes the next state itself, so state is model-written but checked by votes. One full run reported, authors' own system, not peer reviewed in the text read. Models with tool access excluded.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: collapse is not a hard limit when state is kept small and each step is voted. Supports a design where the model does one step and code or votes guard it. It does not show the model can find the algorithm.

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) MAKER - small model and error decorrelation
finding: Small non-reasoning models had per-step error rates comparable to reasoning models and were cheaper. Errors across independent runs were decorrelated: in two runs of 10K sampled steps there were zero steps with errors in both.
numbers: Projected cost for 20 disks at t=0.95: gpt-4.1-mini $3.5K, o3-mini low $9.4K, gpt-oss-20B $1.7K, deepseek-v3.1 $14.6K, kimi-k2 $22.9K, haiku-4.5 $71.2K; llama-3.2-3B error rate 1.0 (cannot be fixed by voting).
limits: Cost is a projection from the paper's Eq. 18 using measured error rates. A model with p below 0.5 per step cannot be rescued by voting.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a deployable small model works if its per-step success is above one half. Measure p per step before choosing the model.

source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey, Bhattacharya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Tested the Einstellung effect on LLMs with six complex and six shortcut equivalence problems. Results are tiny-N and mixed; problem order changed accuracy in some models. Chain of thought raised accuracy but also raised the step count on shortcut items.
numbers: 6 problems per condition, exact match. GPT-4o few-shot: shortcut 0.33, shortcut after complex 0.66, complex 0.66, complex after shortcut 0.83. Llama-3.1-70b: 0, 0.16, 0, 0.66. Llama-3.1-8b: 0.16, 0, 0, 0. With chain of thought, Llama-8b 0.5, 0.66, 0.33, 0.83.
limits: Six items per cell; no statistics. Cell values move in ways that do not match the human pattern (complex-first often helped). Not usable as evidence for or against an Einstellung effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: weak. No clean demonstration of fixation in LLMs from this paper. Do not build on it.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles (NazoNazo benchmark)
finding: On insight-like riddles that need a change of representation, models do far worse than people. Many failures are not failures to generate the right answer. The model wrote the correct candidate in its thinking and then did not endorse it.
numbers: 201 riddles; human reference on 120 items, n=126, mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6 to 59.2). 38 LLMs, zero-shot, no retrieval: non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6% on the human subset. Verification failures were 5% to 39% of a model's wrong answers.
quote: models generate a correct intermediate candidate but fail to endorse it as their final answer
limits: Japanese wordplay, one riddle family. Thought-log reading is qualitative. The strongest model approached the human range.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: supports a separate verify-and-stop step. It does not test a forced restructure operator, so that part of gap 8 stays open. Impasse from state alone is not tested here.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? Confidence elicitation (ICLR 2024)
finding: Verbalised confidence is overconfident and a weak predictor of failure. Consistency across samples helps some. Even the white-box method is only slightly better.
numbers: Verbalised confidence mostly 80% to 100% (multiples of 5). Failure-prediction AUROC about 0.522 for black-box vs 0.605 for white-box (abstract). Five models incl. GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat, five dataset types. Vanilla verbalised ECE averaged above 0.377 for GPT-3.5 and Vicuna in their table.
limits: 2023-era models. Calibration on question answering, not on agent steps.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a confidence-only trigger for escalation would be near chance on failure prediction. Favours explicit signals (failed check, no legal move, repeated state).

source: Yang et al. (2026) Think Fast and Slow: step-level cognitive depth adaptation (CogRouter)
finding: A trained router that picks among four depths per step beat fixed thinking and a binary fast/slow switch on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, with 62% fewer tokens. The signal that trains the choice is action confidence. It is RL training, not a prompt scaffold.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B: 82.3% success; +40.3 over GPT-4o, +18.3 over o3, +14.0 over GRPO. Binary thinking/non-thinking switching still 19.3 points below on Qwen2.5-7B and 18.5 on Llama3.1-8B. Test sets 200 simulations each.
limits: Requires training. Does not compare confidence triggers with impasse triggers. A case study mentions escalation when the observation is unexpected, which resembles an impasse, but that is anecdote.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no head-to-head. Evidence is that step-wise depth beats task-wise depth, and that a binary switch is not enough. Our scaffold cannot train the router.

source: HiAgent authors (2025) HiAgent: hierarchical working memory with subgoals (ACL 2025)
finding: Writing a subgoal before acting helped, but replacing finished subgoals with a short summary and keeping the full trace retrievable helped more. This is evidence about subgoal memory, not about stack depth.
numbers: GPT-4, five long-horizon tasks: success 42% vs 21% average (twofold). Tyreworld: standard 10%, subgoal-only 40%, HiAgent 60%; removing observation summarisation cut success by 30 points, removing trajectory retrieval by 10 points. Jericho: progress rate +23.94%, context tokens -35%.
limits: Success rates come in steps of 10, so probably about 10 episodes per task, unconfirmed. Ablation on one task (tyreworld). No test at stack depth 5 or more.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: explicit subgoals in the prompt are better than none, and pruning finished-goal detail adds more. A written goal stack is plausible but untested at depth.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Don't Get Lost in the Trees (FETCH) - tree search vs best-of-N on GSM8K and MATH
finding: With a trained verifier on a fine-tuned Llama-3-8B, plain tree searches reach accuracy near verifier-weighted voting at 1 to 10 times the tokens. Their fix (state merging, variance reduction) cuts search tokens by up to 3x with similar accuracy.
numbers: GSM8K: best-of-N .753 and weighted voting .819 at 0.83k tokens; BFS .824 at 2.47k; state merging cut BFS from 2.47k to 0.88k tokens. MATH: BoN .340 and weighted voting .352 at 2.44k tokens; best searches .38 to .40 at 2.0k to 66.6k tokens.
limits: The PDF table is garbled (row labels separated from numbers), so row pairing is my reading. Learned verifier, math only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 2: even with a learned verifier, search at matched tokens beats voting by about 0 to 4 points on GSM8K and 3 to 5 on MATH, while costing more tokens unless state merging is used. Merge duplicate states.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual tasks (arithmetic in base 9 and chess legality)
finding: Changing the rule set while keeping the structure drops accuracy a lot, so surface form and familiarity carry weight. Worked examples recover much of the loss.
numbers: GPT-4, 2-digit addition, 0-shot with step-by-step: base 10 98.2%, base 9 38.6% (without step-by-step 100.0% vs 23.4%). With 1, 2, 4, 8 in-context examples in base 9: 48.1, 67.0, 79.7, 85.8%. Claude and PaLM-2 are in the same table.
limits: Not a Kotovsky isomorph design. It changes a rule base, and the results are from an older model generation. Chess opening legality was also tested, numbers only in figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: closest LLM analogue to move-demonstration effects. A handful of worked examples closes most of a representation gap at a small token cost. Still no direct test of operator-compatibility transfer.
